subject: Chemistry

units.title: A: Nature of Science in Chemistry

outcomes.text: Spot common reasoning fallacies and biases that weaken scientific thinking.
Weigh the pros and cons of ethical issues in making and using chemicals.
Break a scientific argument into claims, counterclaims, rebuttals, premises, conclusions and assumptions.
Use oxidation numbers to recognise oxidation and reduction.
Use changes in oxidation number to balance chemical equations.
Define redox, oxidation, reduction and disproportionation by electron transfer.
Pick out the reducing agent in a redox reaction.
Describe what oxidising and reducing agents do in a redox reaction.
Explain the activity series of metals and how it links to ease of oxidation.
Judge whether a redox reaction will happen from the activity series or data.
Describe how the Winkler method measures biochemical oxygen demand as a sign of water pollution.
Explain how electrolytic cells use electrical energy to drive chemical change.
Predict which substances form at the electrodes from the electrolyte, redox series and concentration.
Relate the Faraday constant, Avogadro constant and electron charge to solve problems.
Calculate charge passed and the mass or volume of product in electrolysis.
Find the Avogadro constant from an electrolysis experiment.
Define standard electrode potential and standard cell potential.
Describe the standard hydrogen electrode and how potentials are measured.
Combine two electrode potentials to get a cell potential and predict reaction direction.
Rank oxidising and reducing strength from electrode potentials.
Build redox equations from half-equations.
Explain how concentration changes electrode potential, using the Nernst equation.
Explain how a voltaic cell turns spontaneous redox energy into electricity, with anode and cathode roles.
Explain the Cu-Zn galvanic cell as an example of a voltaic cell.
Explain the common ion effect with examples.
Use ionisation extent and Ka to tell strong from weak acids.
Use ionisation extent and Kb to tell strong from weak bases.
Explain what a buffer is, how it is made, how it controls pH and why blood uses a bicarbonate buffer.
Calculate ion concentrations of slightly soluble salts.
State what the partition coefficient means.
Calculate a partition coefficient for a solute shared between two solvents.
Explain how solute and solvent polarity affect the partition coefficient.

subtopics.title: pH and the ionic product of water

outcomes.text: State pH as the negative log of hydrogen ion concentration and reverse it.
Know that one pH unit means a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.
Use the ionic product of water at 298 K to solve problems.
Sketch pH curves for acid-base titrations.
Describe trends in Group 2 elements and their oxides, hydroxides and carbonates.
Explain how Be, Mg and Ca react with oxygen, water and acids.
Explain Group 2 reactivity from electron configuration.
Describe everyday and industrial uses of Group 2 compounds.
Compare Group 2 elements with Group 1.
Explain the reactivity series and use it to predict reactions.
Apply the reactivity series to predict reaction outcomes.
Explain how metals from this group are extracted and purified.
Explain thermal decomposition and its use in analysing carbonates and nitrates.
Apply thermal decomposition to Group 2 carbonates and nitrates.
Explain solubility trends of Group 2 sulfates and hydroxides using hydration and solution enthalpies.
Explain complex ions and their link to Group 2 compounds.
Explain basic oxides and their uses.
Describe the trend in thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates, using ionic radius and polarisation.
Describe solubility and enthalpy-of-solution trends of hydroxides and sulfates through hydration enthalpy and lattice energy.
Give the general physical and chemical properties of transition metals.
Define a transition element as a d-block element with stable ions having incomplete d orbitals.
Sketch the shapes of the 3dxy and 3dxz orbitals.
Identify properties of transition elements: variable oxidation states, catalysis, complexes, coloured compounds.
Explain variable oxidation states from similar 3d and 4s energies.
Explain catalytic behaviour from several oxidation states and accessible vacant d orbitals.
Explain complex formation through vacant, accessible d orbitals.
Describe ligand reactions forming copper(II) and cobalt(II) complexes with water, ammonia, hydroxide and chloride.
Define a ligand as a lone-pair donor forming a dative bond to a metal.
Use monodentate ligands such as water, ammonia, chloride and cyanide.
Use bidentate and polydentate ligands such as diaminoethane, ethanedioate and EDTA.
Define a complex as a metal centre surrounded by ligands.
Describe linear, square planar, tetrahedral and octahedral complex shapes and angles.
State what coordination number means.
Predict a complex ion's formula and charge from metal, ligand and coordination number.
Explain ligand exchange qualitatively, for example with copper(II) complexes.
Use E-values to predict whether transition-metal redox reactions are feasible.
Analyse reactions of manganate(VII) with ethanedioate, with data and calculations.
Analyse reactions of manganate(VII) with iron(II) in acid, with data and calculations.
Analyse reactions of copper(II) with iodide using suitable data.
Do calculations for other redox systems.
Explain why transition elements form coloured compounds through non-degenerate d orbitals.
Describe d-orbital splitting in octahedral and tetrahedral complexes and the role of energy gap.
Explain colour from absorbed light frequency as an electron moves between d orbitals.
Describe how different ligands change the energy gap, absorbed light and observed colour.
Use copper and cobalt complexes with water and ammonia to illustrate colour and ligand effects.
Describe cis-trans and optical isomerism in transition metal complexes.
Deduce the overall polarity of complexes.
Define the stability constant Kstab of a complex ion.
Write the Kstab expression for a complex.
Use Kstab expressions in calculations.
Explain ligand exchange using Kstab values.
Explain stereoisomerism and its split into geometrical and optical types.
Describe cis-trans isomerism in alkenes, caused by restricted rotation about pi bonds.
Describe benzene and aromatic molecule shapes with sp2 hybridisation and delocalised pi bonding.
Explain what a chiral centre is and how it gives two enantiomers.
Describe how enantiomers share properties except for rotating polarised light and biological activity.
Use the terms optically active, racemic mixture and meso compound on structures.
Describe how two optical isomers affect plane polarised light.
Explain why chirality matters in making drugs, including separating racemates and chiral catalysts.
Explain the shape of benzene and its stability.
Define resonance, resonance energy and relative stability.
Compare how reactive benzene is with alkanes and alkenes.
Describe halogen substitution of benzene and predict ortho, para or meta products.
Explain nitration of benzene, including the nitronium ion, and predict products.
Explain Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation and the Lewis acid role.
Explain side-chain oxidation forming benzoic acid.
Explain hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane with a metal catalyst.
Describe electrophilic aromatic substitution and predict products from substituent directing effects.
Describe how halogenoarenes are produced.
Compare reactivity of chloroethane and chlorobenzene.
Predict products of halogenoalkane reactions from conditions and structure.
Analyse halogenoalkane reaction pathways and use retro-synthesis to find starting materials.
Describe SN1 and SN2 mechanisms, including inductive effects of alkyl groups.
Know that primary halogenoalkanes use SN2, tertiary use SN1, and secondary use a mix.
Explain different halogenoalkane reactivities through C-X bond strengths.
Describe reactions with acyl chlorides to form esters.
Describe making phenol from phenylamine through a diazonium salt.
Recall phenol reactions with bases, sodium, diazonium salts, dilute nitric acid and bromine water.
Explain why phenol is acidic.
Compare the acidity of water, phenol and ethanol.
Explain why reagents and conditions for reacting phenol differ from those for benzene.
Recall that the hydroxyl group of phenol directs substitution on the ring.
Apply phenol chemistry to other phenolic compounds such as naphthol.
State how benzoic acid is made from methylbenzene.
Describe how carboxylic acids react to form acyl chlorides.
Recognise that methanoic and ethanedioic acids can be oxidised.
Explain relative acidities of carboxylic acids.
Explain how chlorine substituents change acidity of carboxylic acids.
Recall how esters are made, such as ethyl ethanoate and phenyl benzoate.
Recall reagents and conditions that turn carboxylic acids into acyl chlorides.
Describe acyl chloride reactions with water, alcohols, phenol, ammonia and amines.
Describe the addition-elimination mechanism of acyl chloride reactions.
Explain why acyl chlorides hydrolyse more easily than aryl chlorides.
Recall how primary and secondary amines are made from halogenoalkanes, amides and nitriles.
Describe how nitriles are made from halogenoalkanes.
Recall how hydroxynitriles form from aldehydes or ketones with HCN.
Describe hydrolysis of nitriles with acid or alkali.
Describe the basicity of aqueous amine solutions.
Describe the reactions of phenylamine, including bromination.
Describe how phenylamine becomes a diazonium salt and then phenol.
Explain relative basicities of ammonia, amines and phenylamine.
Describe azo coupling and the use of azo compounds as dyes.
Describe how amides are made from acyl chlorides.
Describe amide hydrolysis and reduction to amines.
Explain why amides are much weaker bases than amines.
Describe acid-base properties of amino acids.
Describe forming peptide bonds.
Predict electrophoresis results for amino acid mixtures.
Explain chemistry and properties of polymers such as PVC and nylon, and their uses.
Describe condensation of ammonia or amines with acyl chlorides.
Explain the role of chemical industries in Pakistan's economy and its raw materials.
Describe addition and condensation polymerisation, including polyesters and polyamides.
Identify the polymer, monomer or repeating unit from given data.
Deduce the repeating unit of a polymer, or monomers in a section of one.
Predict the type of polymerisation from the monomer.
Explain problems of disposing non-biodegradable polymers.
Recognise that poly(alkenes) are chemically inert.
Recognise that some polymers can be degraded.
Recognise that polyesters and polyamides can be broken down by hydrolysis.
Outline polymers used to make artificial implants and organs.
Describe how artificial intelligence tools help design organic molecules and syntheses.
Explain how carbohydrates are classified and linked to structure.
Explain carbohydrates' roles in health and disease.
Identify the nutritional value of carbohydrates and their role in energy storage.
Explain why humans and animals store glycogen and fat for energy.
Identify complex carbohydrates that lubricate joints.
Explain how proteins are classified and linked to structure.
Describe proteins' roles in body functions and nutrition.
Describe enzymes as biocatalysts.
Identify factors that affect enzyme activity.
Explain how inhibitors affect enzyme-catalysed reactions.
Describe fibrous proteins in hair and silk.
Explain how cholesterol and amino acids act as hormone sources.
Identify insulin as a protein hormone whose lack causes diabetes.
Identify how lemon juice precipitates milk proteins by lowering pH.
Describe how lipids are classified and linked to structure.
Identify the nutritional and biological importance of lipids.
Identify the structural components of DNA and RNA.
Tell the structures of DNA and RNA apart.
Relate DNA sequence to storing genetic information.
Relate RNA sequence to passing information into protein.
Identify sources of minerals such as iron and calcium.
Describe roles of iron, calcium, phosphorus and zinc in nutrition.
Explain the role of minerals in structure and function.
Identify calcium as needed for blood clotting.
Explain that measurements carry random errors and uncertainties.
Justify that random errors propagate and enlarge final uncertainty.
Analyse how experimental design causes systematic errors in one direction.
Justify that repeating trials reduces random but not systematic errors.
Use graphs to show how one variable affects another and find quantities.
Discuss sketched graphs with labelled but unscaled axes for qualitative trends.
Discuss drawn graphs with labelled, scaled axes and measured data.
Analyse mass spectra using m/e values and isotopic abundances.
Calculate relative atomic mass from a mass spectrum.
Deduce an organic molecule's molecular mass from its spectrum.
Suggest what fragments give mass spectrum peaks.
Deduce the number of carbon atoms from the M+1 peak.
Deduce bromine and chlorine from M+2 peak patterns.
Explain the index of hydrogen deficiency to count rings and multiple bonds.
Explore how mass spectrometry, IR and NMR help identify compounds.
Interpret a simple infrared spectrum.
Deduce possible structures of organics from IR spectra and formula.
Predict whether a molecule absorbs in the UV or visible range.
Predict the colour of a transition metal complex.
Explain atomic emission and absorption spectra.
Analyse the carbon environments shown in a 13C NMR spectrum.
Use a 13C NMR spectrum to deduce possible structures.
Predict the number of peaks in a 13C NMR spectrum.
Analyse proton environments in a 1H NMR spectrum.
Use a proton NMR spectrum to read proton types, number and neighbours.
Deduce possible structures from proton NMR data.
Predict chemical shifts and splitting patterns for a molecule.
Explain why TMS is the NMR reference standard.
Recognise why deuterated solvents are used in NMR.
Describe how O-H and N-H protons are identified using D2O.
Describe stationary phase, mobile phase and retention in chromatography.
Explain principles and uses of thin-layer, gas and liquid chromatography.
Interpret Rf values and retention times to find composition.
Explain how to choose conditions for good separation.
Describe combining mass spectrometry with chromatography in forensic analysis.
Explain how material properties suit them to desired structures.
Explain extracting metals from ores.
Explain how catalysts work and why they remain unchanged.
Explain challenges of recycling and toxicity of materials.
Explain how X-ray crystallography analyses structures.
Explain therapeutic index and therapeutic window for drugs.
Explain how aspirin and penicillin work and their chemistry.
Describe opiates and opioid receptors in the brain.
Describe stomach pH regulation and active metabolites.
Recognise the challenge of treating viral infections and how antivirals work.
Identify types of pesticides, their modes of action, benefits and risks.
Identify reactions when acid rain meets crops and soil and effects on yield.
Explain basics of genetic engineering in agriculture, with benefits and risks.
Explain how climate changes affect crop growth and yield.
Justify the importance of environmental protection.
Describe chemical processes in industry, including polymerisation, and product uses.
Identify raw materials of industrial chemistry, including those found in Pakistan.
Explain applications of industrial chemistry in petrochemicals and cosmetics.
Describe safety measures in industrial chemical processes.
Analyse experiment risks and suggest ways to reduce hazards.
Develop lab guidelines that include safety measures.
Communicate lab safety rules to peers.
Analyse chemical hazards by their effect.
Use titrations such as manganate(VII), iron(II), nitrite, ethanedioate and thiosulfate-iodine as examples.
Set up a burette correctly.
Recognise why a rough titration comes first.
Repeat titrations until results agree.
Choose and use suitable indicators.
Investigate rate by mixing reagents and timing an observation.
Suggest experimental designs to measure rate.
Prepare a sample for gravimetric analysis.
Carry out gravimetric analysis with suitable techniques.
Ensure good observations by controlling variables and taking precise measurements.
Prepare a sample for thermometric analysis.
Use and read thermometers accurately.
Set up a gas volume experiment.
Measure gas volume using a gas syringe or burette.
Choose suitable methods for qualitative tests on inorganic ions.
Perform organic tests such as Tollens' reagent, iodine and manganate(VII).
Choose the best way to present collected data.
Interpret experimental data and draw conclusions.
